13→ 14→Hexi is a lightweight, header-only C++23 library for safely handling binary data from arbitrary sources (but primarily network data). It sits somewhere between manually memcpying bytes from network buffers and full-blown serialisation libraries. 15→ 16→Some of the protocols Hexi is used to handle include [DNS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_Name_System), [STUN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STUN), [NAT Port Mapping Protocol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAT_Port_Mapping_Protocol), [Port Control Protocol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Control_Protocol), World of Warcraft (emulators) and GameSpy (emulators). Of course, nothing stops you from defining your own! 17→ 18→The design goals are ease of use, safety when dealing with untrusted data and in the face of programmer mistakes, a reasonable level of flexibility, and keeping overhead to a minimum. 19→ 20→What Hexi doesn't offer: versioning, conversion between different formats, handling of text-based formats, unloading the dishwasher. 21→ 22→Hexi is dual-licensed under MIT and Apache License, Version 2.0. This means you can use Hexi under the license you prefer. 23→ 24→ 25→ 26→Incorporating Hexi into your project is simple! The easiest way is to simply copy `hexi.h` from `single_include` into your own project. If you'd rather only include what you use, you can add `include` to your include paths or incorporate it into your own CMake project with `target_link_library`. To build the unit tests, run CMake with `ENABLE_TESTING`. 27→ 28→Here's what some libraries might call a very simple motivating example: 29→ 30→```cpp 31→#include 32→#include 33→#include 34→#include 35→ 36→struct LoginPacket { 37→ uint64_t user_id; 38→ uint64_t timestamp; 39→ std::array ipv6; 40→}; 41→ 42→auto deserialise(std::span network_buffer) { 43→ hexi::buffer_adaptor adaptor(network_buffer); // wrap the buffer 44→ hexi::binary_stream stream(adaptor); // create a binary stream 45→ 46→ // deserialise! 47→ LoginPacket packet; 48→ stream >> packet; 49→ return packet; 50→} 51→ 52→auto serialise(const LoginPacket& packet) { 53→ std::vector buffer; 54→ hexi::buffer_adaptor adaptor(buffer); // wrap the buffer 55→ hexi::binary_stream stream(adaptor); // create a binary stream 56→ 57→ // serialise! 58→ stream << packet; 59→ return buffer; 60→} 61→``` 62→By default, Hexi will try to serialise basic structures such as our `LoginPacket` if they meet requirements for being safe to directly copy the bytes. Now, for reasons of portability, it's not recommended that you do things this way unless you're positive that the data layout is identical on the system that wrote the data. Not to worry, this is easily solved. Plus, we didn't do any error or endianness handling. All in good time. 63→ 64→ 65→ 66→The two classes you'll primarily deal with are `buffer_adaptor` and `binary_stream`. 67→ 68→`binary_stream` takes a container as its argument and is used to do the reading and writing. It doesn't know much about the details of the underlying container. 69→ 70→To support containers that weren't written to be used with Hexi, `buffer_adaptor` is used as a wrapper that `binary_stream` can interface with. As with `binary_stream`, it also provides read and write operations but at a lower level. 71→ 72→`buffer_adaptor` can wrap any contiguous container or view that provides `data` and `size` member functions. From the standard library, that means the following can be used out of the box: 73→- [x] std::array 74→- [x] std::span 75→- [x] std::string_view 76→- [x] std::string 77→- [x] std::vector 78→ 79→Plenty of non-standard library containers will work out of the box, too, as long as they provide a vaguely similar API. 80→ 81→The container's value type must be a byte type (e.g. `char`, `std::byte`, `uint8_t`). `std::as_bytes` can be used as a workaround if this poses a problem. 82→ 83→ 84→ 85→Hexi supports custom containers, including non-contiguous containers. In fact, there's a non-contiguous container included in the library. You simply need to provide a few functions such as `read` and `size` to allow the `binary_stream` class to be able to use it. 86→ 87→`static_buffer.h` provides a simple example of a custom container that can be used directly with `binary_stream`. 88→ 89→ 90→ 91→As mentioned, Hexi is intended to be safe to use even when dealing with untrusted data. An example might be network messages that have been manipulated to try to trick your code into reading out of bounds. 92→ 93→`binary_stream` performs bounds checking to ensure that it will never read more data than the buffer has available and optionally allows you to specify an upper bound on the amount of data to read. This can be useful when you have multiple messages in a buffer and want to limit the deserialisation from potentially eating into the next. 94→ 95→```cpp 96→buffer_t buffer; 97→// ... read data 98→hexi::binary_stream stream(buffer, 32); // will never read more than 32 bytes 99→``` 100→ 101→ 102→ 103→The default error handling mechanism is exceptions. Upon encountering a problem with reading data, an exception derived from `hexi::exception` will be thrown. These are: 104→ 105→- `hexi::buffer_underrun` - attempt to read out of bounds 106→- `hexi::stream_read_limit` - attempt to read more than the imposed limit 107→ 108→Exceptions from `binary_stream` can be disabled by specifying `no_throw` as an argument. This argument eliminates exception branches at compile-time, so there's zero run-time overhead. 109→```cpp 110→hexi::binary_stream stream(buffer, hexi::no_throw); 111→``` 112→Regardless of the error handling mechanism you use, the state of a `binary_stream` can be checked as follows: 113→```cpp 114→hexi::binary_stream stream(buffer, hexi::no_throw); 115→// ... assume an error happens 116→ 117→// simplest way to check whether any errors have occurred 118→if (!stream) { 119→ // handle error 120→} 121→ 122→// or we can get the state 123→if (auto state = stream.state(); state != hexi::stream_state::ok) { 124→ // handle error 125→} 126→``` 127→ 128→ 129→ 130→In the first example, reading our `LoginPacket` would only work as expected if the program that wrote the data laid everything out in the same way as our own program. 131→This might not be the case for reasons of architecture differences, compiler flags, etc. 132→ 133→Here's the same example but doing it portably. 134→```cpp 135→#include 136→#include 137→#include 138→#include 139→#include 140→#include 141→ 142→// an example structure that has separate serialise and deserialise functions 143→struct LoginPacket { 144→ uint64_t user_id; 145→ std::string username; 146→ uint64_t timestamp; 147→ uint8_t has_optional_field; 148→ uint32_t optional_field; // pretend this is big-endian in the protocol 149→ 150→ // deserialise Whenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware.
